questions.question: A student observes pollen grains dancing randomly under a microscope when suspended in water. If the water is replaced by a slightly thicker liquid at the same temperature, what is the best explanation of what happens to this motion?
options: The motion stops completely because the water molecules have disappeared.
The motion continues but becomes slower because the thicker liquid's particles collide with the pollen differently.
The motion accelerates because thicker liquids contain more energetic particles.
The pollen grains dissolve completely, meaning no motion can be observed.

questions.question: If a drop of blue food dye is carefully placed at the bottom of a still beaker of water, it slowly spreads out without being stirred. Which statement best describes the final state of the mixture?
options: The dye particles will eventually settle back at the bottom due to gravity.
The dye particles will eventually achieve a completely uniform, random distribution throughout the water.
The dye particles will cluster in the middle where there is less water pressure.
The dye particles will only spread if the water is heated to its boiling point.

questions.question: In an experiment, a student adds a drop of ink to hot water and another drop to cold water. The ink spreads much faster in the hot water. Why does this happen?
options: The particles in the hot water move more quickly, colliding with and dispersing the ink faster.
Hot water particles are larger, which pushes the ink particles further apart.
The hot water has less gravity acting on it, allowing the ink to rise.
The cold water particles have stopped moving entirely, blocking the ink.

questions.question: A student mixes a spoonful of flour into water and stirs it. Initially, the liquid looks cloudy. After leaving it on the desk for an hour, they notice a layer of flour at the bottom and clear water above. What does this tell us about the mixture?
options: It is a solution, because the flour has completely dissolved into the water.
It is a suspension, because the solid particles were visible and eventually settled over time.
It is a pure substance, because the flour and water have chemically combined.
It is a solution, because the particles have reached a permanent random distribution.

questions.question: Why does a solid lump of sugar not dissolve instantly the moment it touches water?
options: The water molecules must first freeze the sugar to break it apart.
The forces of attraction holding the sugar particles together must be overcome by interactions with the water.
The sugar particles are too heavy to be moved by the lightweight water molecules.
The sugar must melt into a liquid before it can mix with any solvent.

questions.question: A student measures 50 cm³ of ethanol and 50 cm³ of water. When they mix them together in a measuring cylinder, the total volume is recorded as 97 cm³ instead of 100 cm³. What is the most scientifically accurate explanation for this observation?
options: Some of the liquid particles evaporated instantly due to a chemical reaction.
One type of particle is smaller and fits into the spaces between the other type of particle.
The measuring cylinder shrunk when the two liquids were mixed together.
Mass was lost during the physical mixing process, reducing the volume.

questions.question: Which of the following scenarios describes a key difference between the process of melting and the process of dissolving?
options: Melting requires only heat to change state, whereas dissolving requires interaction with a solvent.
Melting is a chemical change that creates new substances, while dissolving is a physical change.
Dissolving requires heat to break chemical bonds, while melting can happen at any temperature without energy.
Melting only happens to pure substances, whereas dissolving only happens to mixtures.

questions.question: A student dissolves 15 g of salt into 100 g of water in a sealed flask. What will be the total mass of the resulting salt solution?
options: Exactly 115 g, because the masses of the mixed substances add together and mass is conserved.
Slightly less than 115 g, because the salt particles fit into the spaces between water particles.
Slightly more than 115 g, because the salt particles react and gain mass from the air.
Exactly 100 g, because the dissolved salt no longer has any measurable mass.

questions.question: A student wants to measure exactly 12.5 cm³ of acid for a titration where precision is critical. Why should they choose a burette instead of a beaker?
options: A beaker is designed for heating liquids, so it cannot hold acid safely.
A burette is designed for precise volume delivery, and using the wrong equipment impacts the quality of results.
A beaker cannot hold volumes of liquid that are not whole numbers.
A burette chemically reacts with the acid to make it easier to see.

questions.question: A chemist heats a clear liquid and observes that it begins to boil at exactly 100°C, and the temperature remains constant at 100°C until all of it has boiled away. What does this tell them about the liquid?
options: The liquid is a mixture because it boiled at a single temperature.
The liquid is a pure material because it has a fixed boiling point.
The liquid is an unstable compound that is decomposing.
The liquid must be a solution of salt and water.

questions.question: Road grit (salt) is spread on icy roads in winter. How does this help clear the ice, based on physical properties?
options: The salt acts as a blanket, keeping the ice warm so it melts.
The salt acts as an impurity, lowering the melting point of the water so it melts at a lower temperature.
The salt reacts chemically with the ice, releasing heat that melts it.
The salt absorbs the water, turning the ice directly into a gas.

questions.question: A sample of wax is heated slowly, and its temperature is recorded. The wax begins to melt at 45°C, but does not completely turn into a liquid until the temperature reaches 52°C. What does this indicate about the wax?
options: The wax is a pure material that has a high heat capacity.
The wax is a mixture, which causes it to melt over a range of temperatures.
The thermometer being used is faulty and cannot read a fixed temperature.
The wax is undergoing a chemical decomposition rather than melting.

questions.question: A student keeps adding spoonfuls of sugar to 100 ml of water at room temperature. After 5 spoonfuls, no more sugar dissolves, even after stirring for 10 minutes. Why did the sugar stop dissolving?
options: The sugar molecules have bonded with each other to form an indestructible solid.
At a given temperature, there is a limit to how much solute can dissolve in a solvent.
The water molecules have evaporated, leaving no room for the sugar.
The student did not stir fast enough to break the water's chemical bonds.

questions.question: A hot, saturated solution of copper sulfate is left on a windowsill to cool down. After several hours, blue crystals are seen at the bottom of the beaker. What process explains this?
options: The copper sulfate reacted with the glass beaker to form a new compound.
As the solution cooled, the solute became less soluble and crystallized out.
The solvent expanded, pushing the solute out of the solution.
The cooling process melted the copper sulfate, turning it back into a solid.

questions.question: After plotting points for solubility versus temperature on a scatter graph, a student draws a smooth curve that passes close to most of the points. What is the primary purpose of drawing this line of best fit?
options: To connect every single data point directly to show experimental errors.
To help identify and describe the overall relationship between the two variables.
To change the actual experimental values to make the data look perfect.
To show that the independent variable did not affect the dependent variable.

questions.question: A student investigates how the temperature of water affects the solubility of salt. Which of the following is the most complete and scientifically sound conclusion for this investigation?
options: 'The temperature of the water increased as I heated it with the Bunsen burner.'
'As the temperature of the water (independent variable) increased, the amount of salt that dissolved (dependent variable) also increased.'
'Salt dissolves very well in water because water is a good solvent.'
'The amount of salt dissolved stayed at 35 grams because we used a balance to measure it.'

questions.question: A student wants to dissolve a tablet of medicine as quickly as possible. Based on scientific principles, which combination of changes would most likely increase the rate and amount of dissolving?
options: Crush the tablet into a powder and use hot water instead of cold water.
Keep the tablet whole and use cold oil instead of warm water.
Crush the tablet and use a smaller volume of cold water.
Keep the tablet whole and stir it very slowly in a saturated solution.

questions.question: In an experiment to find out how the type of solvent affects how much sugar can dissolve, a student uses water, ethanol, and propanol. What is the independent variable in this investigation?
options: The mass of sugar that dissolves.
The type of solvent used.
The temperature of the room.
The volume of solvent used.

questions.question: A student measures how long it takes for 5 grams of salt to dissolve in water at different temperatures. What is the dependent variable in this investigation?
options: The temperature of the water.
The time taken for the salt to dissolve.
The mass of the salt used.
The volume of the water.

questions.question: A student wants to test if stirring speed affects how fast sugar dissolves. They set up two beakers: Beaker A has 100 ml of hot water and is stirred quickly; Beaker B has 50 ml of cold water and is stirred slowly. Why is this not a fair test?
options: Because they used two different beakers which made the measurement of time impossible.
Because they changed multiple variables (temperature, volume, and stirring speed) instead of only changing the stirring speed.
Because stirring speed cannot be measured with standard school laboratory equipment.
Because sugar dissolves at the same rate regardless of temperature or volume.

questions.question: Under a microscope, pollen grains suspended in water are seen moving erratically. Why do these visible pollen grains move randomly?
options: Because they are being randomly bumped and pushed by the invisible, fast-moving water particles around them.
Because the pollen grains themselves are living organisms that actively swim in all directions.
Because the pollen grains are undergoing a chemical reaction with the water, causing them to self-propel.
Because the water molecules have melted, creating empty gaps that pollen grains fall into randomly.

questions.question: If a drop of food coloring is carefully placed at the bottom of a completely still beaker of water, after several days the color is evenly distributed without any stirring. What explains this?
options: Because gravity pulls the food coloring particles up and down until they are chemically destroyed.
Because liquid particles are free to move and will eventually reach a random, uniform distribution throughout.
Because the food coloring particles melt into the water particles, losing their individual mass.
Because the food coloring particles are heavier than water, causing them to eventually float to the top and stay there.

questions.question: A student stirs a spoonful of flour into water. The mixture looks cloudy, but after an hour, a layer of white flour forms at the bottom and the liquid above is almost clear. What type of mixture is this, and why?
options: It is a solution, because the flour has completely dissolved into its respective atoms.
It is a pure substance, because the flour and water have undergone a physical state change to become a single gas.
It is a suspension, because the solid particles remain visible and eventually settle to the bottom over time.
It is a saturated solution, because cooling the mixture caused the flour particles to melt.

questions.question: When a solid solute is added to a solvent, what energetic barrier must be overcome first for dissolving to actually occur?
options: The solute particles must be melted by raising the solvent's temperature to its boiling point.
The air pressure acting on the surface of the solvent must be completely eliminated.
The chemical bonds inside the water molecules must be broken down into hydrogen and oxygen.
The attractive forces holding the individual solute particles together must be overcome.

questions.question: A student carefully measures 50 cm³ of pure ethanol and 50 cm³ of pure water. When they mix them together, the total volume of the mixture is only 96 cm³. What is the scientific explanation for this observation?
options: Some of the mass of the ethanol was destroyed during the chemical reaction.
Particles of one substance fit into the empty spaces between the particles of the other substance.
The ethanol particles melted the water particles, reducing their individual volumes.
The mixture became a pure substance with a much higher density and lower mass.

questions.question: A student states: 'When sugar is stirred into hot tea, it melts because the tea is hot.' How should a teacher correct this misconception?
options: Dissolving requires a solvent to interact with and disperse the solute, whereas melting only requires heat to change a solid to a liquid.
Melting is a chemical change that creates new substances, while dissolving is a physical change.
Sugar cannot dissolve in hot liquids; it can only melt when it is cooled down to room temperature.
Dissolving is a physical process, whereas melting is a chemical process that destroys the mass of the sugar.

questions.question: Why is it vital to write a scientific method with precise quantities, specific equipment, and clear step-by-step instructions?
options: To guarantee that the dependent variable changes in exactly the same way regardless of the control variables.
To convert the physical process of dissolving into a permanent chemical reaction.
To ensure that the investigation can be repeated by the same person, and reproduced by different people, to get similar results.
To make sure that the total mass of the mixture is greater than the sum of the individual masses.

questions.question: A student dissolves 15 g of salt into 100 g of water in a sealed beaker. What will be the total mass of the resulting salt solution?
options: Slightly less than 115 g, because some of the salt mass is lost when its particles fit into the spaces of water.
Exactly 100 g, because the salt dissolved and therefore its mass is no longer present.
More than 115 g, because a chemical reaction occurred which created extra mass.
Exactly 115 g, because the mass of the mixed substances adds together and mass is conserved.

questions.question: A student wants to measure exactly 45 cm³ of a liquid solvent to investigate how fast a solute dissolves. Which piece of equipment and unit should they use?
options: A measuring cylinder, measuring in cm³.
A balance, measuring in grams.
A thermometer, measuring in °C.
A beaker, measuring in grams.

questions.question: A sample of a white solid is heated slowly. It begins to melt at exactly 114 °C and is completely liquid at 114 °C. What does this sharp, fixed melting point suggest about the solid?
options: It is a mixture of several different substances with different densities.
It is a pure material made of only one type of substance.
It is a suspension that has settled over time.
It is an impure substance containing a high concentration of dissolved gases.

questions.question: Water normally freezes at 0 °C. When salt is added to water, the mixture now freezes at -4 °C. Why does this change occur?
options: The salt acts as a catalyst that speeds up the chemical destruction of the water.
Salt is a pure substance that has a fixed melting point of -4 °C.
The presence of impurities, like salt, changes the melting and freezing points of the substance.
The salt particles have melted into the water, increasing the total volume of the water.

questions.question: You are heating a liquid substance in a lab. It starts boiling at 78 °C, but as you continue heating, the temperature steadily rises to 95 °C while it continues to boil. What does this tell you about the liquid?
options: It is a pure substance that is undergoing a rapid chemical reaction.
The thermometer is broken because pure materials always boil at a steadily increasing temperature.
It is a suspension where the solid particles are settling to the bottom.
It is a mixture, because mixtures boil over a range of temperatures rather than a single fixed point.

questions.question: A student keeps adding spoonfuls of sugar to 100 cm³ of water at 20 °C. Eventually, no matter how much they stir, the sugar just sits at the bottom. What does this demonstrate?
options: At any given temperature, there is a limit to how much solute can dissolve in a solvent.
The sugar has melted and turned into a gas, which pushed the liquid out.
The water has become a pure material with a fixed boiling point.
The forces of attraction between water molecules have become infinitely strong.

questions.question: A student dissolves 50 g of a substance in 100 cm³ of hot water at 80 °C. As the solution cools down to 20 °C, they notice solid crystals starting to appear at the bottom. Why does this happen?
options: The water particles have shrunk, squeezing the solute particles out of existence.
The solute becomes less soluble and can turn back into an insoluble solid as the solution cools.
The cooling process has caused a chemical reaction that created new mass.
The solute has melted because the temperature decreased.

questions.question: After plotting their results on a scatter graph of solubility versus temperature, a student draws a smooth curve through the points. How does this line of best fit help the student?
options: It automatically corrects any errors they made in measuring the mass of the solute.
It proves that the independent variable was not controlled during the test.
It helps them to identify and describe the relationship between temperature and solubility.
It shows that the mixture has a fixed melting point and is therefore pure.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most complete and scientifically sound conclusion for an investigation into how temperature affects the solubility of salt?
options: Salt dissolves very quickly when you stir it, because stirring is a physical process.
The temperature of the water was kept at 40 °C throughout the entire fair test.
A measuring cylinder was used to measure 50 cm³ of water because it is accurate.
As the temperature of the water (independent variable) increases, the mass of salt that dissolves (dependent variable) increases.

questions.question: A student wants to increase how much of a solid solute can dissolve in a liquid. Which set of factors could affect the solubility of this substance?
options: The size of the solute pieces, the choice of solvent, or the temperature of the solvent.
The size of the beaker, the color of the spatula, or the room's air pressure.
The mass of the balance, the 2D drawing style of the equipment, or the time of day.
Whether the mixture is a suspension or a pure substance with a fixed boiling point.

questions.question: A student investigates how changing the type of solvent (water, ethanol, or propanone) affects how much of a food dye dissolves. What is the independent variable in this investigation?
options: The mass of food dye that dissolves.
The type of solvent used.
The temperature of the room.
The volume of the measuring cylinder.

questions.question: When investigating how the temperature of water affects the solubility of sugar, a student uses the same volume of water (100 cm³), the same brand of sugar, and the same stirring speed each time. What are these kept-the-same factors called?
options: Independent variables.
Dependent variables.
Control variables.
Random variables.

questions.question: In an investigation to see if solute particle size affects how quickly it dissolves, why must the student keep the solvent temperature, solvent volume, and stirring speed exactly the same?
options: To make sure the total mass of the mixture is less than the sum of the individual masses.
To prevent the solute from turning into a pure substance with a fixed melting point.
To allow the liquid particles to stop moving completely so that Brownian motion can occur.
To ensure it is a fair test, so that only the particle size is changed and any effect on dissolving time is clearly due to it.
